notes.meaning: A perfumer makes costly, fragrant oil, but even a few tiny dead flies rotting inside will turn the sweet smell into a foul stench. In the same way, a single foolish act can quickly ruin a fine reputation built over many years of wise living. A person of honor must be especially watchful, because small sins cause great damage to a good name.

other.label: Catholic
other.view: Early Latin church tradition, following Jerome, read the dead flies as evil thoughts planted in a believer's mind by Beelzebub, whose name means lord of flies.

notes.meaning: In ancient times, the right hand was a symbol of strength, skill, and favor, while the left hand stood for weakness and clumsiness. Solomon explains that a wise person's mind is ready to direct daily choices toward what is good and safe. A fool lacks this inner guidance, so his impulses constantly lead him in the wrong direction.

A foolish person cannot keep his true character hidden for very long. Even in simple daily routines like walking down a public road, his foolish speech and strange behavior give him away. Everyone who passes by can easily see that he lacks good sense.

other.label: Catholic
other.view: The Latin Vulgate translation understood the phrase to mean that the fool in his arrogance thinks everyone else he meets is a fool.

notes.meaning: When an angry ruler or employer flares up in temper, the natural human urge is to quit one's post or walk away in anger. Solomon advises staying faithful to duty and answering with humble, quiet patience instead of fighting back. A gentle, composed spirit calms fierce tempers and keeps minor disputes from turning into major rebellions.

Solomon points out another painful wrong observed in earthly life. It happens when a supreme ruler makes a serious error in judgment. The king uses his power poorly by failing to put the right leaders in positions of authority.

Rulers often promote foolish and unworthy people to high offices of honor and trust. At the same time, those who are rich in wisdom, integrity, and good judgment are demoted or left in lowly stations. Such favoritism harms the entire community by leaving society poorly led.

Riding on horseback was an ancient sign of royalty and high public honor. Solomon describes an upside-down world where unqualified servants ride proudly like kings, while true nobles must walk in the dust like servants. It shows how earthly status is frequently handed to those least capable of wielding power well.

Pits dug to trap other people often end up trapping the person who dug them. Tearing down an old garden wall to seize property also risks disturbing venomous snakes nesting in the cracks. Deceitful schemes and destructive acts usually bounce back to hurt the schemer.

Honest labor like quarrying large stones or chopping heavy logs carries real physical hazards. Heavy stones can slip and crush the worker, and woodcutters can be injured by flying splinters or slipping tools. Hard work requires constant caution and practical wisdom to avoid needless harm.

Chopping wood with a dull axe forces a laborer to swing with extra muscle, wasting energy and risking injury. Taking time to sharpen the blade first allows the work to get done smoothly and easily. Wisdom works like a sharpened edge, guiding human effort so that skill achieves what brute force cannot.

In the ancient East, snake charmers used soft tunes and whispers to calm dangerous snakes before touching them. If a charmer waits too long and gets bitten before working his charm, all his professional skill does him no good. In the same way, a quiet slanderer strikes with verbal poison before anyone has a chance to stop him.

A wise man speaks with kind and thoughtful words that win favor and encourage listeners. By contrast, a fool speaks without thinking, uttering reckless gossip and angry boasts. His own careless words eventually bring ruin upon him.

A foolish person's speech starts out silly and shallow. As he continues to babble, his talk grows into reckless rage and harmful madness. Unchecked, foolish words reveal an undisciplined mind that brings misery to everyone nearby.

Even though a fool knows very little, he chatters on endlessly about things he cannot understand. No human being can predict the future or know what will happen after this life, yet the fool speaks boldly as if he knows it all. True wisdom keeps quiet when facing the unknown.

Knowing the way to the city was an ancient proverb for knowing the most obvious, well-marked road. A fool exhausts himself with fruitless labor because he lacks even basic common sense to guide his steps. Hard work accomplishes nothing without the simple wisdom to do things right.

A nation suffers deep distress when its king is immature and lacks sound judgment. Morning was the customary time for rulers to administer justice, hear public complaints, and conduct state business. When princes spend their mornings feasting and drinking instead of working, the whole country falls into neglect.

A land is blessed and secure when its king shows true nobility of character and self-control. Good rulers wait to feast until their public responsibilities have been fulfilled. They eat and drink to gain physical strength for daily service, rather than indulging in wild drunkenness.

When a homeowner is too lazy to repair roof beams, the roof sags and rainwater leaks into the house until the whole structure collapses. This everyday picture illustrates what happens to an entire nation when its rulers neglect their duties. Ignoring small repairs and responsibilities always leads to widespread decay.

Feasts are held to bring laughter, and wine gives brief cheer to human life. In practical daily matters, money is needed to buy food, host banquets, and keep the affairs of a home or government running. This statement describes how the earthly world operates, rather than offering a spiritual promise of wealth.

Even when rulers make serious mistakes, Solomon cautions subjects not to curse them, not even in secret thoughts or private bedrooms. Words spoken in quiet places have a surprising way of spreading quickly, as if carried to powerful ears by a little bird. Guarding one's speech and thoughts keeps a person safe from sudden danger.
